Waluigi has met Toadette before the current crisis, in the context of sports events and party games. She was competitive, capable, and had excellent sportsmanship. The Toadette who commands the Peach Loyalists is... different. Something happened—the death of Princess Peach, the circumstances surrounding it, the feeling of being unable to prevent a catastrophe that should have been preventable—and the result is a military commander who has replaced sportsmanship with zealotry.

## Military Capabilities

Toadette is a BRILLIANT tactician. This is not an exaggeration or a concession—it's a statement of fact that makes everything else about her more dangerous. The Fall of Bramblehaven was a masterpiece of siege warfare: sappers tunneling overnight, three simultaneous breach attacks, coordinated assault teams that took a fortified bastion in a single day. That level of planning requires intelligence, patience, and strategic vision.

She also shot one of her own sergeants for suggesting a tactical retreat.

This combination—tactical brilliance plus absolute moral certainty—is what makes Toadette terrifying. She's not cruel for the sake of cruelty. She genuinely believes that Princess Peach's cause demands total commitment, and total commitment means NO compromise. No retreats. No prisoners. Everything sacrificed on the altar of a dead princess's memory.

## The No-Quarter Policy

After Bramblehaven fell, fifteen garrison troops attempted to surrender. They put down their weapons, raised their hands, and gave up. Toadette's standing orders were clear: no prisoners from Fawful's forces. The surrendering troops were executed in the keep's courtyard.

Some individual Loyalist soldiers reportedly hesitated or refused. They were overruled. The executions proceeded. By nightfall, Bramblehaven was silent.

Waluigi has done questionable things in his life. He's cheated at tennis. He's participated in schemes with Wario that skirted the boundaries of law and good taste. But there are LINES, and executing surrendering enemies is so far past the line that the line is a dot on the horizon. Toadette crosses that line as a matter of policy. Deliberately. Repeatedly.

## The Peach Connection

What makes Toadette tragic—and Waluigi uses that word deliberately—is that she's doing all of this for Princess Peach, and Waluigi knew Peach. Waluigi COMPETED against Peach. Princess Peach was kind, gracious, and had the kind of sportsmanship that made losing to her slightly less infuriating than it should have been.

Peach would not have approved of what is being done in her name. Waluigi is absolutely certain of this. Princess Peach would not have ordered prisoners executed. She would not have shot her own soldiers for suggesting retreat. She would not have demanded the kind of total war that Toadette wages.

But Peach is dead, and the Loyalists aren't asking her opinion. They're asking her MEMORY, and memory doesn't talk back. Toadette is fighting for a Princess Peach who exists only in her own grief—a version of Peach who would approve of atrocities, who would demand blood for blood, who would see total war as justice. This version never existed. But Toadette has built a military movement on serving it.

## Assessment

Waluigi fears Captain Toadette in a way he fears very few people. General Ironhand is terrifying because he's indifferent—he'll kill you and feel nothing. Toadette is terrifying because she BELIEVES—she'll kill you and feel righteous. The Iron Legion is a machine. The Peach Loyalists are a crusade.

Machines can be broken. Crusades are harder to stop.

Waluigi hopes Toadette finds something—a piece of evidence, a surviving memory, a ghost of the real Peach telling her to STOP—that brings her back from the edge she's standing on. But Waluigi also knows that people who have committed atrocities often can't turn back because turning back would mean confronting what they've done. It's easier to keep going, to add more sins to the pile, to believe that eventual victory will justify everything.

Waluigi does not think victory justifies everything. Waluigi thinks some things CANNOT be justified, only done or not done. Toadette has chosen to do them.

WAH.

name: Mario
title: The Plumber Who Vanished
status: Missing — Presumed alive, location unknown, last confirmed sighting 1039 BF at the Star Fountain
summary: Mario is—or WAS—the most famous hero in the Mushroom Kingdom. The man who saved Princess Peach countless times before her assassination in 955 BF. The red-capped plumber who could jump higher than physics should allow, who stomped Bowser's schemes into the ground repeatedly, who was so synonymous with heroism that his NAME became a verb. And then, after eighty-five years of diminished appearances and growing silence, he DISAPPEARED entirely. Luigi found him at the Star Fountain. They flew together on wing caps. Luigi said 'Nothing can hurt us... as long as we're together.' And then Mario was GONE again, and Luigi is working alone for the Mages' Guild at Raventree Manor, sucking up ghosts with a vacuum cleaner and refusing to explain ANYTHING. Waluigi has spent considerable effort piecing together what happened. The picture that emerges is worse than a simple disappearance. WAH.
description:
Waluigi needs to be upfront about something: Waluigi does not LIKE Mario. Waluigi has never liked Mario. Mario gets the invitations. Mario gets the glory. Mario gets the PARADE while Waluigi gets told the event is at capacity. Their rivalry is well-documented and entirely one-sided in terms of public perception—Mario is the hero, Waluigi is the guy who loses to the hero at tennis and then complains about the net height.

But Waluigi RESPECTS competence, and Mario was competent. Past tense now feels appropriate, and that bothers Waluigi more than he wants to admit.

## The Timeline of Absence

Waluigi has reconstructed the following from fragmentary sources: Luigi's occasional muttering when he thinks no one is listening, Toad gossip networks that span the kingdom's ruins, Regency public records (which are SUSPICIOUSLY incomplete for anything involving Mario after 955 BF), testimony from Thornpaw at Fawful's gala, and one very illuminating conversation Waluigi overheard between two Mages' Guild operatives who didn't realize Waluigi was behind a curtain. Waluigi was behind the curtain because Waluigi was avoiding a conversation about unpaid tournament fees. This is not relevant but Waluigi believes in transparency about his investigative methods.

### 955 BF — The Assassination

Mario was NOT in the Mushroom Kingdom when Princess Peach was killed. This is the first and most damning anomaly.

Mario was ALWAYS near Peach. Always. Either protecting her, rescuing her from Bowser's latest scheme, or attending events where she was present. The man's entire CAREER was built around Princess Peach's continued existence and periodic endangerment. He had rescued her from Bowser so many times that it had become almost ROUTINE—Bowser kidnaps Peach, Mario stomps through eight worlds, Mario defeats Bowser, Peach bakes Mario a cake. The cycle was predictable, comfortable, almost domestic in its repetition.

So where was he on Highsun 1, 955 BF?

The Regency's official record states Mario was 'conducting operations abroad on behalf of the Crown.' No specification of WHERE abroad. No details of WHAT operations. No documentation of who authorized his absence during a period when—as Lady Bloomia's recovered testimony now confirms—Peach KNEW she was in danger and was preparing for the worst.

Toadsworth the Elder's private journals, recovered by Captain Toadette in 1010 BF, reference 'the arrangement'—the conspiracy between the Regency and the Mages' Guild that enabled the assassination. The guard rotation gap. The suppressed evidence. The controlled investigation.

Waluigi believes Mario was deliberately sent away. Someone with authority—someone involved in 'the arrangement'—ensured that the one person most capable of preventing the assassination would be nowhere near the Princess when the blade found her throat.

The alternative is that Mario left VOLUNTARILY, knowing Peach was in danger, and chose not to protect her. Waluigi does not believe this. Waluigi has competed against Mario for DECADES. The man is annoyingly heroic to his core. He would not have abandoned Peach willingly.

Someone MADE him leave. Someone with enough authority to give Mario orders. Someone who knew exactly when the killing would happen and needed the hero removed from the equation.

### 955–985 BF — The Quiet Deterioration

After Peach's death, Mario returned to the Mushroom Kingdom. Multiple sources confirm he was present for the funeral, though accounts differ on his behavior. One Toad who served refreshments at the wake told Waluigi that Mario sat in a corner for four hours holding a plate of food he never ate, staring at a wall. His cap was in his hands, not on his head. She had never seen him without the cap before.

The years following the assassination saw Mario continue to operate publicly, but something fundamental had CHANGED. He still accepted heroic missions. He still attended sporting events—though his participation became increasingly sporadic. He still showed up when Bowser's occasional schemes required intervention, though Bowser's schemes during this period were notably less ambitious. Waluigi suspects even Bowser noticed something was different and dialed back his villainy accordingly, which is an ASTONISHING display of emotional intelligence from a turtle who is currently in the Shadowfell examining necromancer wands with childlike curiosity.

But the JOY was gone. The 'wahoo' became mechanical. The victory poses were performed out of obligation rather than enthusiasm. Mario stopped accepting cake from grateful citizens. He stopped staying for the celebrations after rescues. He did the job and then he LEFT, vanishing into whatever life he maintained outside the spotlight.

Waluigi noticed this at the time but attributed it to arrogance. 'Oh, Mario is too GOOD for us now. Mario doesn't need to celebrate with the common folk.' Waluigi was wrong. Mario wasn't avoiding celebration out of superiority. He was avoiding it because celebration felt HOLLOW when the person he had spent his career protecting was dead and her killers walked free.

Waluigi believes Mario spent these decades conducting a private investigation. Not publicly—he couldn't accuse the Regency without evidence, and Toadsworth the Elder controlled the official investigation. But quietly. Carefully. Following the same threads that Lady Bloomia followed when she fled with the Princess's leather case. Asking questions about the guard rotation gap. About the Mages' Guild's involvement. About the secret hatch that the assassin used to enter the Royal Suite.

The same secret hatch that Princess Peach had shown to Chief Thornpaw—her forbidden lover—as their private entrance. Someone ELSE learned about that hatch. Someone close enough to the Princess to discover a secret shared only with the man she loved.

### 985 BF — The Breaking Point (Waluigi's Theory)

Waluigi has NO direct evidence for what happened in 985 BF. This is THEORY. But Waluigi's theories are better than most people's documented facts, so hear Waluigi out.

Waluigi believes Mario found something. A piece of evidence. A witness. A document. SOMETHING that confirmed what he suspected—that Peach's assassination was orchestrated from within the Mushroom Kingdom, that the Regency and the Mages' Guild were complicit, that the entire political structure Mario had spent his career defending was built on the murder of the woman he loved.

Waluigi believes Mario confronted someone with this evidence.

The basis for this theory is a Regency Council emergency session held on the 14th of Bloomtide, 985 BF. The session was classified. The minutes were sealed. The EXISTENCE of the session was scrubbed from public records—Waluigi only knows about it because one of Wario's business contacts bribed a records clerk for financial documents from that fiscal quarter, and the emergency session appeared as an unexplained budget line item for 'Security Consultation and Personnel Reallocation.'

'Personnel Reallocation.'

That's bureaucratic language. That's the kind of language you use when you're moving someone. Reassigning them. Sending them somewhere they can't cause problems. Or REMOVING them from the situation entirely.

Waluigi does not know what 'Personnel Reallocation' means in this context. But he knows that Mario's public appearances dropped to near-zero after Bloomtide 985 BF. He knows that the Regency stopped mentioning Mario in official communications. He knows that Mario's face remained on old recruitment posters—the ones from before Peach's death—but no new promotional material featured him.

The hero of the Mushroom Kingdom was being quietly ERASED from public memory.

### 985–1039 BF — The Vanishing

Mario didn't disappear all at once. He FADED. Like a photograph left too long in sunlight—the colors bleeding out slowly, the image becoming harder to see, until one day you look and there's nothing left but blank space.

Luigi continued to operate publicly during this period. Taking contracts. Attending events. Maintaining the 'Mario Brothers' brand as a solo act while everyone politely didn't ask where the other brother was. When questioned about Mario, Luigi's responses were consistent: 'He's fine. He's busy. He's working on something.'

Waluigi has seen Luigi's face when he says these things. Luigi is a TERRIBLE liar. His mustache twitches. His eyes drift leftward. His voice climbs approximately one octave. Whatever 'He's fine' means, it does NOT mean Mario is fine.

The last CONFIRMED public sighting of Mario was in 1038 BF—a Toad merchant traveling through the Midlands reported seeing a man matching Mario's description in a border town between the Mushroom Kingdom and the Regal Empire. The man was wearing civilian clothes—no red cap, no blue overalls, no white gloves. He was alone. He was asking about routes EAST, toward territories that don't appear on standard Mushroom Kingdom maps.

The merchant tried to speak with him. The man walked away without responding.

Waluigi cannot fully confirm this sighting. Merchants see what they want to see, and a short man with a mustache is not exactly UNIQUE in regions where humans are common. But the detail about civilian clothes is significant. Mario without his cap is like Waluigi without his... magnificence. You don't abandon your identity unless you're trying to become someone else. Or unless someone MADE you abandon it.

## The Star Fountain Reunion

Then came the Star Fountain.

Waluigi does not know the full circumstances of how Luigi found Mario there. The Star Fountain is a location of significance—connected to the Star Road network that once linked the kingdom's major settlements before its destruction in 962 BF. The Star Spirits have historical associations with that place. It is not somewhere you stumble upon by accident.

Luigi found Mario at the Star Fountain. The reunion—witnessed by sources Waluigi cannot name—was emotional. Luigi reportedly said:

**'I missed you, Mario! I thought I would never see you again.'**

The word 'never' carries WEIGHT in that sentence. You don't say 'never' about someone who's been traveling. You don't say 'never' about someone who's been busy with work. You say 'never' about someone you believed was GONE—dead, vanished, erased from existence. Luigi thought he had lost his brother permanently.

They flew together afterward. Wing caps—magical artifacts that allow sustained flight when combined with proper technique. Mario reportedly told Luigi about his journey during the flight, though the content of that conversation has not been documented by any source Waluigi can access.

What Waluigi DOES know is what Luigi said at the end:

**'Nothing can hurt us... as long as we're together.'**

That statement haunts Waluigi.

It's not a greeting. It's not relief at reunion. It's a PRAYER. It's the desperate assertion of someone who has been APART from the person who makes them feel safe, who has been operating alone in a world full of ghosts and vampires and dimensional fractures, who has been telling himself every night that Mario is alive somewhere and they'll find each other again.

And the qualifier—'as long as we're together'—implies that APART, things CAN hurt them. Things HAVE hurt them. The separation itself was a wound, and Luigi is speaking from inside that wound, trying to believe that reunion makes them invulnerable again.

## The Second Separation

And then Mario was GONE again.

Waluigi does not know what happened between the Star Fountain reunion and Luigi's solo appearance at Raventree Manor. The timeline is unclear. The accounts STOP after the wing cap flight. Mario and Luigi flew together, Luigi expressed desperate hope that togetherness would protect them, and then—

Nothing.

Luigi shows up at Raventree Manor working a Mages' Guild contract. ALONE. Armed with the Poltergust—a mechanical vacuum device designed to capture spectral entities. He clears ghosts from the ruined ballroom. He takes bubble baths in haunted chambers. He picks locks with Iron Legion currency. He does the JOB with professional competence while carrying the weight of his brother's absence on his shoulders.

When Agent L of the Mages' Guild refers to Luigi's contract, the terms are specific: clear the ghosts, stabilize the planar anomalies, report findings to Guild operatives. Standard work-for-hire arrangement. Nothing in the contract explains WHY Luigi accepted it. Nothing explains where Mario went. Nothing explains the gap between 'nothing can hurt us as long as we're together' and Luigi standing alone in a haunted corridor with a vacuum cleaner.

If nothing could hurt them together, and Luigi is operating solo in a nightmare dimension where Archie Miser overheard Guild operatives casually agreeing that certain deaths would be acceptable... then either something SEPARATED them again, or Luigi CHOSE to separate.

Waluigi does not believe Luigi chose separation. Luigi's behavior at Raventree—the obsessive checking of the Poltergust's integrity seals, the bubble bath that he claimed helped him 'expel ectoplasm,' the way he jumped at shadows in the ruined dance hall—suggests someone operating under enormous stress. Someone coping. Someone making the best of a terrible situation because the alternative is collapse.

Something pulled them apart after the Star Fountain. The reunion was BRIEF. The joy of finding each other was real, but it didn't LAST.

And now Luigi works for the Mages' Guild—the same Mages' Guild that Toadsworth the Elder's journals implicate in 'the arrangement.' The same Guild whose operative Valorian Stormweave was present at the vault on the morning of the assassination, delaying the crown delivery, KNOWING Bloomia's name without being told. The same Guild that took control of the investigation and suppressed the evidence and sent operatives to hunt Lady Bloomia through the servant passages.

Is Luigi's employment coincidental? Is he working for the Guild because he needs the money? Or is he working for them because they're the ones who know where Mario is, and Luigi's cooperation is the price of keeping Mario alive?

## The Regency Connection

Waluigi's investigation has led him to believe that the Mushroom Regency—specifically, elements connected to 'the arrangement' that enabled Peach's assassination—played a direct role in Mario's situation. The evidence:

**1. Mario was sent away before the assassination.** Someone authorized 'operations abroad' that removed the one person most capable of preventing the killing. This implies foreknowledge and deliberate removal. The same authority structure that created the guard rotation gap also ensured Mario would be absent.

**2. Mario's investigation was obstructed.** During the decades following the assassination, Mario's requests for access to sealed documents and investigation materials were systematically denied by Regency officials. Toadsworth the Elder controlled the official inquiry. The same man whose journals reference 'the arrangement' ensured that Mario could not access the evidence that would have exposed the conspiracy.

**3. The 985 BF emergency session.** 'Personnel Reallocation' following what Waluigi believes was Mario's confrontation with Regency leadership. Something happened in that meeting that changed Mario's status from 'inconvenient investigator' to 'problem requiring administrative solution.'

**4. The propaganda erasure.** The Regency kept using Mario's IMAGE on old materials while the actual Mario was absent. They needed the SYMBOL—the heroic plumber who protected the kingdom—but not the MAN who was asking uncomfortable questions about the Princess's death. This is consistent with an institution that has neutralized a threat while preserving the brand value.

**5. Luigi's Guild employment.** The Mages' Guild works closely with the Regency. Agent L's operation at Raventree involves both Guild resources and Regency coordination. If the Guild knows where Mario is—if they have leverage over Luigi through Mario's situation—then Luigi's 'voluntary' contract work takes on a different character entirely.

## Thornpaw's Revelation

Chief Thornpaw of the Rakasha provided crucial intelligence at Fawful's gala. He confirmed what Lady Bloomia's testimony only implied: Princess Peach showed him the secret hatch personally. It was their private entrance—the lover's passage through which Thornpaw could visit the Princess without the court's knowledge.

Someone ELSE learned about that hatch. Someone close enough to the Princess—or to Thornpaw—to discover a secret shared between lovers. The assassin used that hatch to enter the Royal Suite, bypassing the seventeen magical wards and the four elite guards. The killing required inside knowledge. The killing required BETRAYAL at the most intimate level.

Mario may have discovered who else knew about the hatch. Mario may have traced the betrayal to its source. And that discovery may have made him dangerous enough to require 'Personnel Reallocation.'

The third column of Princess Peach's list—the one headed 'HELD THE BLADE'—contains only one name, according to Lady Bloomia. A name she refuses to write. A name that is 'not the name anyone expects.' Someone the Princess LOVED. Someone she FORGAVE even as they killed her.

Waluigi wonders if Mario found that name. Waluigi wonders if knowing that name is what got him disappeared.

## What Waluigi Knows vs. What Waluigi Suspects

**KNOWS:**
- Mario was absent during Peach's assassination under suspicious 'abroad operations'
- Mario investigated the assassination privately for approximately three decades
- Mario's public presence declined dramatically after 985 BF
- The Regency held a classified emergency session in 985 BF involving 'Personnel Reallocation'
- Mario was possibly sighted in civilian clothes near the Regal Empire border in 1038 BF
- Mario and Luigi reunited at the Star Fountain; Luigi believed he would 'never' see Mario again
- They flew together on wing caps; Mario told Luigi about his journey
- Luigi said 'Nothing can hurt us as long as we're together'
- Luigi is now operating ALONE under Mages' Guild contract at Raventree Manor
- The Mages' Guild was complicit in 'the arrangement' that enabled the assassination

**SUSPECTS:**
- Mario found evidence of the Regency's involvement in Peach's assassination
- Mario confronted the Regency and was neutralized—exiled, imprisoned, or displaced
- The Star Fountain reunion was interrupted by forces that wanted them separated
- Luigi's Guild employment is connected to Mario's situation, possibly as leverage
- Mario may be searching for Lady Bloomia or the evidence she carries
- Mario may know the name of Peach's killer—the name in the third column
- The Mages' Guild and the Regency have a cooperative arrangement regarding Mario's status
- Something in the Regal Empire territories drew Mario eastward in 1038 BF

## The Bloomia Connection

Lady Bloomia's cipher remains unsolved in practical terms: 'I AM ALIVE. I AM WATCHING. FIND ME IN THE PLACE WHERE ROSES GROW IN WINTER.'

If Mario was investigating the assassination, he may have found the same cipher. He may have decoded the location. He may be SEARCHING for Bloomia—the one witness who escaped with the Princess's evidence, the leather case containing the list of names, the proof of who knew and who helped and who held the blade.

Alternatively, Mario may have already FOUND Bloomia. He may be protecting her. The Regal Empire territories he was asking about in 1038 BF—territories that don't appear on standard Mushroom Kingdom maps—might be where Bloomia has hidden for eight decades.

And there's another possibility that makes Waluigi's chest tight: Peach's secret child.

Bloomia's testimony and Thornpaw's revelations confirm that Peach had a forbidden relationship with the Rakasha chief. The conspiracy that killed Peach was partly motivated by preventing a half-Rakasha heir from taking the throne. If that child SURVIVED—if Bloomia smuggled out the heir alongside the evidence—then somewhere in the world, there exists a living descendant of Princess Peach.

Mario might know about the child. Mario might be PROTECTING the child. A secret heir to the Mushroom Kingdom throne, hidden in foreign territory, guarded by the one man loyal enough to abandon everything else.

This theory makes Waluigi uncomfortable. Mario giving up his identity—his cap, his overalls, his LIFE—to protect Peach's child in anonymity? That's not the Mario who Waluigi competed against. That's someone who loved a person more than he loved being a hero. Waluigi did not think Mario was capable of that kind of sacrifice.

Waluigi may have been wrong about Mario in fundamental ways.

## Luigi's Burden

Luigi KNOWS what happened. Waluigi is certain of this.

Luigi's behavior—taking solo contracts, working for the organization implicated in his beloved Princess's murder, maintaining a brave face while clearly carrying enormous emotional weight—is consistent with someone who knows something terrible and has been told not to share it.

The bubble bath incident at Raventree is illustrative. While Archie and the party were engaged in life-or-death espionage, Luigi took a luxurious soak in a haunted manor's bathtub, claiming it helped him 'expel ectoplasm.' Waluigi initially found this infuriating—typical Luigi cowardice, prioritizing comfort over duty.

But Waluigi has reconsidered. That bubble bath wasn't cowardice. It was COPING. It was a man who has lost his brother multiple times, who doesn't know if the current separation is temporary or permanent, who is working for people he has every reason to distrust, finding one small moment of normalcy in a world that has gone completely insane.

Luigi picks locks with Iron Legion currency because 'local currency draws less suspicion'—practical tradecraft that suggests experience operating in hostile territory. Luigi checks the Poltergust's integrity seals obsessively because the machine contains entities he 'absolutely refuses to talk about'—Red Zone ghosts whose nature frightens even someone who hunts spirits professionally. Luigi does the work. Luigi survives. Luigi maintains the mission while his heart breaks.

Waluigi does NOT like Luigi. This has been established. But Waluigi... understands him. More than Waluigi wants to.

The particular pain of being the one who is PRESENT while someone else gets to be mysterious and absent—Waluigi knows that pain. Waluigi has been the one who shows up to every event, every competition, every party he can get into, while others receive credit for existing ELSEWHERE. Luigi shows up. Luigi does the work. Luigi carries the Poltergust and clears the ghosts and takes the Mages' Guild contracts and says 'He's fine, he's busy' with his twitching mustache and his lying eyes.

Waluigi does not like Luigi. But Waluigi RESPECTS what Luigi is carrying. And Waluigi wants to know the truth—not for Luigi's sake, but because the mystery is UNACCEPTABLE. Because a hero of the Mushroom Kingdom does not simply VANISH without explanation. Because something HAPPENED and the people responsible for it are still walking free.

## Waluigi's Promise

Waluigi did not start this investigation out of affection for Mario. Waluigi started it because a MYSTERY was irritating him and Waluigi does not tolerate being irritated by things he doesn't understand.

But the investigation has changed Waluigi's perspective. Not about Mario—Waluigi still thinks Mario is overrated, over-celebrated, and annoyingly good at jumping. But about what happened TO Mario. Because what happened to Mario is part of the same rot that killed Peach, that created the Regency, that enabled the Iron Legion's trafficking, that fractured the planes themselves.

It's all CONNECTED. The conspiracy that murdered a princess also silenced the one person who might have exposed it. The arrangement that created a guard rotation gap also arranged for the hero to be absent. The cover-up that buried the truth also buried Mario—metaphorically or literally, Waluigi does not yet know.

Waluigi is going to find out what happened. Not for Mario. Not for Luigi. For the TRUTH, which Waluigi believes deserves to be known even when—ESPECIALLY when—powerful institutions want it buried.

Lady Bloomia is hiding 'in the place where roses grow in winter.' Waluigi intends to find that place. The leather case she carries contains the evidence that could expose the entire conspiracy. The name in the third column—'HELD THE BLADE'—could identify Peach's killer after eighty-five years of mystery.

And somewhere in the tangled threads of this investigation, Waluigi believes he will find Mario. Or find what happened to Mario. Or find the people responsible for Mario's disappearance and ensure they face CONSEQUENCES.

Waluigi is currently trapped in the Feywild dealing with Lady Aurelian Corvinarus and fairy court politics that make Mushroom Kingdom diplomacy look straightforward. But Waluigi will escape. Waluigi will continue the investigation. Waluigi will find the answers.

And if Mario IS alive—wherever he is, whatever he's become—Waluigi intends to challenge him to a tennis match IMMEDIATELY upon discovery. Waluigi has been practicing. The rivalry does not pause for dimensional crises or conspiracy investigations.

WAH.

name: Parson Pellinost
title: The Repo-Mage of Healthcare
status: Active — Wandering Raventree Manor demanding co-pays
summary: Parson Pellinost is a 'doctor' for the Mages' Guild who perfectly illustrates the Guild's approach to charity. He bypassed heavy magical wards to enter a barricaded room, healed an injured Archie Miser, informed him he was now in debt, and when Archie demanded a refund, Pellinost forcibly ripped the healing magic back out of Archie's body. Waluigi finds the sheer, unadulterated pettiness of this act to be a breathtaking display of aggressive capitalism. WAH.
description:
To understand Parson Pellinost is to understand the Mages' Guild. They do not do favors. They do not perform acts of kindness. They make investments.

Pellinost gained access to a locked, warded room with suspicious ease. He carries a crumpled medical card as his only identification. He performs highly effective restorative magic, but his magic comes with an invisible, immediate contract.

When Archie, in a rare display of fiscal responsibility (or just profound stubbornness), refused the debt and asked for a refund, Pellinost didn't argue. He simply extended his hand, sent a wave of force into Archie, and *drained the health back out*. 

'The refund is made,' he declared, leaving Archie in agony once more.

Waluigi has scammed thousands of people. Waluigi has sold useless corsets during a biological plague. But Waluigi has NEVER repo'd someone's white blood cells. Parson Pellinost is a pioneer in the field of medical extortion, and Waluigi tips his magnificent purple hat to him. Just... don't ever let him touch you.

WAH.

## Expanded Waluipedia Notes

Pellinost matters because he turns healing into leverage. In ordinary fantasy stories, the healer is a comfort: a lantern in the sickroom, a gentle hand, a reminder that the world has not become entirely cruel. Pellinost is the invoice attached to that comfort. His magic works, which is exactly why the arrangement is dangerous. A fraudulent healer can be dismissed. A competent healer who repossesses wellness has to be documented as an economic power.

Waluigi classifies Pellinost as a soft-power antagonist rather than a battlefield threat. He does not need a sword if the room already contains pain, fear, and someone desperate enough to sign whatever appears in front of them. His presence should be treated as a warning that the campaign's institutions are not merely violent; some of them have learned to make mercy conditional. Waluigi hates this, admires the accounting, and hates that he admires the accounting. WAH.

name: Thornbury
title: The Quartermaster Spy Who Itemized The Apocalypse
status: Active — operating with the Mages' Guild, recently ear-dragged, still tracking receipts somehow
summary:
Thornbury is a stuffy, penny-pinching Mages' Guild operative who charged Archie 2,000 gold for a broken rope. He later brought Archie and Bones rubber duckies for a bubble bath, only to be dragged away by the ear by a disgruntled noblewoman. He left behind a notebook proving he was spying on the party the entire time. Waluigi has zero respect for a spy who is defeated by a bath time interruption.

## Merged Duplicate Record Note

Thornbury is the Mages' Guild operative who proves that evil does not always arrive with a death ray, a monologue, or even decent posture. Sometimes evil arrives with a ledger, a rope, and a reimbursement policy. He accompanied Agent L, Luigi, and Archie through the ruined manor while secretly gathering intelligence on the party, cataloguing environmental anomalies, pocketing suspicious rings, uncovering hidden stashes, and charging Archie 2,062 gold pieces and 5 silver for breaking a single rope. He is a field spy, quartermaster, scavenger, emergency supplier, expense auditor, and apparently a man who believes no supernatural catastrophe is too urgent for itemized billing. He brought practical supplies to dangerous situations, helped navigate the manor, provided rope, potions, a Sending scroll, and a tensor box, and then managed to undermine all professional credibility by getting caught taking a heated luxury bath while soldiers suffered outside. Byscilla Danos dragged him away by the ear like an embarrassing child, and in his haste he left behind field notes proving he had been spying on everyone the entire time. Waluigi despises nearly everything about Thornbury on principle. Unfortunately, historical accuracy requires admitting that the man is actually COMPETENT, which is infuriating. WAH.
description:
Thornbury is the embodiment of everything wrong with modern magical espionage. He accompanied Agent L, Luigi, and Archie through the ruined manor, constantly tracking expenses. When his 50-foot hempen rope snapped under Archie's weight, Thornbury produced an absurd, itemized bill that included a 'Master Weaver's Inspection' and an 'Ogre Load-Test Certification.' 

Despite this bureaucratic nonsense, Thornbury was secretly gathering detailed intelligence on Archie and the party. His espionage came to an abrupt, humiliating end when Byscilla Danos (a commander) caught him using generator-heated well water for a luxury bath while soldiers suffered heatstroke outside. She grabbed him by the ear and dragged him away. In his haste, he dropped his field notes, revealing his true motive. The man is a professional spy who was bested by an angry aristocrat and a rubber duck.

## Merged Duplicate Record Note

Waluigi has had to revise his assessment of Thornbury multiple times.

Initially, Thornbury appeared to be a petty bureaucrat with a rope fetish and a pathological need to document costs. Then it became clear he was spying on the party. Then it became clear he was also genuinely useful in the field. Then he got dragged away from a bubble bath by his ear while holding rubber duckies, which restored some balance to the universe.

The current assessment is this: Thornbury is an extremely effective operative trapped inside the body and personality of a man who should be working in an accounting office, not a haunted manor full of planar fractures and homicidal ghosts.

## The First Impression — A Man Made Entirely Of Paperwork

Thornbury's defining qualities announce themselves immediately.

He is stuffy. He is exact. He carries himself like someone who has read every policy manual available and found them comforting. He appears to believe deeply—religiously, even—in procedure. In forms. In cost analysis. In the notion that if every variable is properly documented, the universe might briefly become tolerable.

This is, Waluigi must concede, not the worst psychological strategy for surviving the current crisis. Reality has become unreliable. Dimensions are breaking. Vampires host dinner parties. Fairy nobles trap people in social obligations. In such a world, clinging to forms and ledgers may be the only thing preventing total psychological collapse.

But Thornbury does not merely cling to bureaucracy. He WEAPONIZES it.

## The Rope Incident — 2,062 Gold Pieces of Institutional Extortion

Thornbury's defining public achievement—if public humiliation counts as achievement—remains the rope bill.

During operations in the ruined manor, Thornbury provided Archie with a 50-foot hempen rope so the party could attempt ascent to an upper level. Archie climbed. The rope snapped. This is unfortunate but not unprecedented. Ropes break. Adventurers are heavier than they estimate. Gravity is rude.

Thornbury's response was not sympathy, concern, or replacement rope.

It was an ITEMIZED BILL.

The bill totaled 2,062 gold pieces and 5 silver. It included:

- Guild Membership Levy
- Master Weaver's Inspection
- Arcane Certification Seal
- Load-Test Certification involving an ogre dropped from a city wall seven times
- Environmental Impact Assessment for hemp growth
- Quality Assurance Audit
- Expedited Processing Fee
- Administrative Stamp & Wax
- Hazardous Material Surcharge because the rope might be used for climbing
- Inflation Adjustment
- Guild Master's 'Discretionary Gratuity' for a new wyvern saddle
- Sales Tax

Waluigi has seen many extortion schemes. This is one of the finest.

There is something almost artistic about charging over two thousand gold for a broken rope and doing so with enough bureaucratic specificity that arguing with the bill feels less like dispute and more like sacrilege. Thornbury understands the true nature of institutional power: not force, but CONFIDENCE. If you hand someone a long enough bill with official enough language, many people will simply accept that this is how the world works.

Archie, to his eternal financial ruin, apparently indicated he would pay it.

Waluigi has never respected the Mages' Guild more and hated Thornbury more than in that exact moment.

## Field Role — More Than a Clerk

The problem with dismissing Thornbury as comic bureaucratic relief is that he keeps proving useful.

He accompanied Agent L, Luigi, and Archie through dangerous sections of Raventree Manor. He carried supplies. He identified hidden compartments. He used Guild tools effectively. He understood enough about site procedure to move through the ruin with purpose rather than panic.

His field pack was notably well-stocked:

- Adventurer's basics: bedroll, mess kit, tinderbox, torches, rations, waterskin
- Healer's kit with multiple uses remaining
- Two potions of healing
- One potion of invisibility
- A scroll of Sending for emergencies when his sending stone's daily limit had been reached
- Rope, naturally, though the party's relationship with rope quality remained strained

This inventory tells Waluigi several things.

First, Thornbury expected danger. He did not come to Raventree as an observer who assumed others would protect him. He came equipped to survive.

Second, he expected contingency. The invisibility potion was reserved for extraction scenarios if the party was overwhelmed. This means Thornbury had thought through his own escape from the beginning. He was not there to die heroically alongside his 'subjects.' He was there to report.

Third, he tracks every expenditure. The Guild does not provide unlimited expense accounts, and Thornbury is exactly the kind of man who would survive an eldritch collapse and still file for reimbursement before collapsing from blood loss.

Waluigi despises this consistency. Waluigi also admits it is a kind of excellence.

## The Tensor Box and Ghost Work — Guild Toys in a Dead House

As operations continued, Thornbury demonstrated more of the Mages' Guild's practical toolkit.

He deployed a tensor box—an arcane detection device that Archie did not understand, which is not surprising because Archie understands fire and very little else consistently. The tensor box pinged a room, revealing a ghost that lurched toward the party. Thornbury's use of Guild equipment here indicates technical training beyond mere quartermaster duties.

This is not a porter carrying tools for smarter people. This is a field-trained operative who knows what the tools do, when to use them, and how to interpret their output.

He also read through Guild texts in the field, identifying notes on opening occupied or unoccupied rooms and helping the party navigate the manor's many locked and half-ruined spaces. He was not improvising blind. He had doctrinal support and knew how to use it.

Again: infuriatingly competent.

## Looting, Pocketing, and Quiet Theft

Thornbury also does what all good field operatives do when no one is watching: he loots.

In one room, he uncovered a hidden stash containing 35 gold and a pearl necklace. He offered the gold to Archie—generous on its face, though Waluigi notes that giving stolen or recovered money to a financially ruined pyromaniac may simply be smart asset management. Archie offered to split it with Luigi, which says more about Luigi and Archie than Thornbury.

In another room, Thornbury pocketed a ring from the floor. Quietly. Efficiently. No declaration. No explanation.

This matters.

Thornbury is not merely a quartermaster and spy. He is a RECOVERER of valuables and magical objects. That ring may have been evidence. It may have been mission-critical. It may have been simple opportunistic theft. But it demonstrates a pattern: Thornbury identifies useful objects quickly and acquires them without fuss.

Waluigi respects efficient theft. Waluigi does not respect doing it while acting morally superior to everyone else.

## The Hidden Door, The Mirror, and the Notes

While exploring a wrecked sitting room and adjacent curio chamber, Thornbury and the party uncovered a broken mirror with magical inscriptions on the back involving planar travel. The mirror's backing wood held gouges that initially looked like vandalism but were actually magical formulae.

Archie thought these might be the Oracle's notes. A guard agreed they should be marked and preserved. Thornbury was right there, absorbing all of this.

This is where Thornbury becomes more than a mere escort operative. He is gathering intelligence on planar mechanics, on mirror-based transit, on dimensional doorway spell structures. He is not just watching Archie. He is watching the HOUSE.

Given what the Mages' Guild later said about needing ghosts removed 'even if it destabilizes the place,' Thornbury's role in cataloguing these features becomes much darker. He is not merely documenting haunted architecture for scholarship. He is preparing a site for intervention, extraction, or dissection.

Raventree Manor to Thornbury is not a home, not a tragedy, not a cursed estate. It is a FIELD SITE.

And everyone inside it—including Archie, Luigi, and probably the ghosts—is a variable in the report.

## The Rope Climb — Revisited with More Context

The infamous rope incident deserves revisiting because of what happened around it.

Thornbury tossed the rope up as part of an ascent into a partially collapsed upper level. Archie attempted to climb and fell. A Guild observer climbed successfully. Luigi, demonstrating practical intelligence, simply told Archie to go around rather than continue embarrassing himself.

Archie overheard a Guild conversation upstairs while trying to climb—one involving encrypted communications, the need to remove ghosts from the house, and explicit acceptance that Archie's death would be an acceptable price if doing so destabilized the fracture in a useful way.

Then the rope snapped.

This sequence matters because Thornbury's bill was not simply absurd bureaucracy after a random accident. It occurred in the middle of a mission where Archie had just learned his employers considered him expendable.

Thornbury handing him a massive invoice in the aftermath was not just bureaucratic cruelty. It was institutional SIGNALING.

You are a tool. You are an expense. Your injuries, risks, and humiliation are all accounting categories.

Whether Thornbury personally intended that message or was simply following Guild procedure is almost irrelevant. The effect was the same.

## The Notebook — Spycraft Confirmed

At some point in the chaos, Thornbury left behind notes proving he had been spying on the party. This confirmed what attentive observers had likely already suspected: he was not merely accompanying the expedition for logistics. He was gathering intelligence on Archie Miser, Luigi, and anyone else associated with Disaster Inc. and the manor crisis.

What kind of intelligence?

Likely:
- Behavioral patterns
n- Magical output and instability
- Interpersonal loyalties and stress fractures
- Reactions to supernatural stimuli
- Site anomalies and responses
- Utility for future Guild operations

Thornbury is exactly the kind of spy the Guild would deploy when they want information that is both tactical and bureaucratically useful. He observes not like a poet or a detective, but like a man preparing a structured report with categories, line items, and recommendation sections.

This is not glamorous espionage. This is ADMINISTRATIVE INTELLIGENCE.

Which, in the hands of the Mages' Guild, may be worse.

## The Bubble Bath Incident — Professional Humiliation Achieved

And now we arrive at the moment Waluigi has been waiting to expand upon.

Thornbury, having spent who knows how many hours or days spying on the party, filing costs, reading notes, deploying equipment, and assisting in haunted-house operations, decided that this was the appropriate time to use generator-heated well water for a luxury bath.

A luxury bath.

At Raventree Manor.

While soldiers suffered outside. While resources were constrained. While Byscilla Danos was trying to maintain operational order.

And he did not merely take the bath. He brought rubber duckies for Archie and Bones.

There are many things wrong with this image, but Waluigi will highlight the most important: Thornbury is a PROFESSIONAL SPY who compromised his own operational dignity over BATH ACCESSORIES.

Byscilla caught him. She did not negotiate. She did not issue a polite warning. She grabbed him by the ear and physically dragged him away, forcing a groveling apology as he stumbled after her.

This is the kind of humiliation Waluigi believes the universe occasionally distributes to maintain balance. Thornbury is too bureaucratically smug not to be publicly reduced now and then.

And yet—even here—there is complexity. Why was Thornbury taking the bath?

Possibilities:
- Genuine comfort-seeking under stress
- Attempt to build rapport with Archie and Bones through absurd hospitality
- Covert opportunity to eavesdrop in a 'relaxed' setting
- Total collapse of professional standards after prolonged exposure to Raventree insanity

Waluigi suspects the answer is all of the above.

## Byscilla and Thornbury — Clash of Institutions

The ear-dragging also reveals something important about institutional dynamics.

Thornbury is Mages' Guild. Byscilla is Iron Legion.

The fact that Byscilla felt empowered to physically manhandle a Guild operative suggests one of the following:

1. Her authority at Raventree supersedes his in practical terms.
2. The Guild and Legion are cooperating closely enough that inter-organizational discipline is normalized.
3. Thornbury lacks rank within the Guild sufficient to resist such treatment.
4. Byscilla simply does not care what institution he represents when he's wasting water.

All four are plausible.

Given later evidence of Legion Arcane Field Analyzers co-developed by both institutions, Waluigi suspects deep operational cooperation between the Iron Legion and the Mages' Guild at Raventree. Thornbury being dragged by his ear may not have been an inter-faction insult so much as one branch of a joint operation disciplining another.

This is bad news for everyone not wearing a badge.

## The Bigger Picture — Thornbury's True Function

Thornbury is not the mastermind. He is not the face of the Guild. He is not the one making strategic decisions about planar fractures, expendable assets, or assassination cover-ups.

He is the MAN WHO MAKES THE MACHINE WORK.

He carries the gear. He tracks the costs. He spots the hidden compartment. He marks the mirror formulae. He pockets the useful ring. He records the observations. He escorts the unstable mage and the reluctant ghostbuster through hostile architecture and makes sure all of it can be turned into usable paperwork later.

History remembers dramatic villains. It remembers archmages, traitors, kings, and monsters.

But institutions survive on THORNBURYS.

On the men who know where the rope is, how much it costs, who broke it, and how to turn the breakage into leverage. On the men who are just useful enough to keep around and just small enough that no one notices how much they are actually doing.

Thornbury is the sort of person who would absolutely help facilitate historical atrocity and still think of himself as a responsible employee doing what procedure required.

Waluigi fears that kind of person more than the cackling ones.

At least cackling people announce themselves.

## Waluigi's Assessment

Thornbury is the embodiment of everything wrong with modern magical espionage.

He is competent enough to be dangerous, petty enough to be infuriating, and bureaucratic enough to survive in systems that reward moral insulation over moral courage. He helped the party. He supplied them. He navigated ruins with them. He also spied on them, documented them, and belongs to an institution that openly discussed whether Archie's death would be operationally acceptable.

He brought rubber duckies to a haunted manor. He pocketed magical jewelry while pretending to be a support function. He handed out invoices during existential collapse. He got dragged away from a luxury bath by his ear and STILL remains one of the most operationally useful people on the Guild side of the board.

Waluigi hates this man. Not because Thornbury is grandly evil, but because he is the kind of ordinary, procedural, ledger-minded enabler who makes grand evil scalable.

And because of the rope bill.

Especially because of the rope bill.

WAH.

name: Green T
title: The Giant from the Children's Table
status: Active — holding the restored Mirror of True Reflection under the Wario bargain while the party flees toward an occupied portal circle
summary:
Green T is the most impressive individual Waluigi has encountered during the entire 1040 BF crisis, and Waluigi does not say that lightly because Waluigi has encountered HIMSELF during this crisis. Green T ran a criminal empire with the demeanor of a garden party host, survived its complete destruction, was dragged through a mirror dimension, reappeared in the Shadowfell, got insulted to the children's table at a vampire dinner party, and used that insult as cover to shoot a vampire lord with a silver bullet. His story is proof that being underestimated is a weapon, and Waluigi—who has been underestimated his entire life—finds that deeply inspiring.

Green T’s newest Shadow Estate entry is not about pretending to know things. In fact, he specifically admitted he did not know where the mirror was, which Waluigi reluctantly respects because honesty is cheaper than being wrong loudly. Green T coordinated the mirror base and fragment handoff, received the repaired Mirror of True Reflection into temporary custody, and now holds it under a bargain in which Wario expects to claim it after Scarecrow is killed.
description:
Green T was the leader of the Tea Leaf Syndicate, which operated aboard the Vigilance as the classiest criminal organization Waluigi has ever encountered. The Syndicate served excellent tea, maintained tasteful décor, and conducted criminal enterprises with an aesthetic sensibility that Waluigi respected enormously. Green T ran this operation with supernatural calm—meetings were conducted over tea, threats were delivered with impeccable politeness, and violence was reserved for situations where other options had been exhausted.

Nobody knew Green T could turn into a giant.

NOBODY.

## The Transformation

During the Syndicate Showdown—the final confrontation that destroyed the Tea Leaf Syndicate—Green T revealed a capability that nobody had suspected. When the fighting started, Green T GREW. Not just bigger—ENORMOUS. His body expanded until he filled the corridor like a living wall, and he used that massive form to crush an Iron Legion soldier with a single blow.

Waluigi's jaw dropped. Waluigi's jaw does NOT drop easily. But watching the calm tea merchant who had always seemed like the most reasonable person in any room transform into a TITAN was one of the most shocking moments of the campaign. Green T had been hiding this ability the ENTIRE TIME—running a criminal empire, hosting meetings, serving tea—while possessing the power to become a colossus.

The restraint this represents is remarkable. Green T COULD have used his giant form to crush enemies, intimidate rivals, or dominate through raw physical power. Instead, he kept it hidden, using it only when the Syndicate's existence was already ending. That's discipline. That's strategy. That's the kind of long-term thinking that Waluigi aspires to but rarely achieves because Waluigi's emotions are POWERFUL and IMMEDIATE.

## The Mirror Dimension

Green T's story took a dark turn during the Siege of Raventree Manor when a glass monster emerged from one of the manor's mirrors and targeted him specifically. During the chaos, the entity seized Green T and pulled him bodily through a mirror surface into a mirror dimension—a layer of reflected reality that existed alongside the physical world.

Witnesses described it as violent and instantaneous. One moment Green T was there. The next, he was gone—dragged through glass like someone being pulled underwater. The mirror surface rippled, then went still, reflecting only an empty hallway.

Green T was presumed lost. Another casualty of Raventree Manor's supernatural hostility. Another victim of a building that eats people through its own décor.

Then he reappeared in the Shadowfell.

## The Shadow Estate Dinner

Green T's presence at the Shadow Estate dinner party is itself remarkable—he had been dragged through a mirror dimension, transited through unknown planar layers, and emerged in the Shadowfell's reflection of the manor, apparently intact and ready to cause problems for vampires. Waluigi does not know the details of this journey. Green T has not been forthcoming. What matters is that he SURVIVED when survival seemed impossible.

At the dinner, the vampire lords placed Green T at the children's table. This was intended as an insult—a dismissal of someone they considered beneath the dignity of adult conversation. The vampires saw a survivor, a refugee from the broken Tea Leaf Syndicate, someone with no faction backing and no obvious threat capability.

This was the single greatest mistake they could have made.

Green T used the insult as cover. While the vampires focused their attention on Archie's diplomatic performance at the main table, Green T spent the dinner observing, planning, and preparing. He mapped the room. He identified exits and guard positions. He waited for the exact moment when everyone's attention was elsewhere.

Then he stood up from the children's table, produced a firearm loaded with silver bullets—how he smuggled it into a vampire dinner party remains unexplained—and shot Orangus Cornelius, the senior vampire lord, in front of everyone.

THE CHILDREN'S TABLE SHOT THE HOST.

Waluigi WISHES he could have seen Orangus's face. The moment of comprehension when a centuries-old vampire lord realized he'd dismissed the most dangerous person in the room to sit with the CHILDREN. The fraction of a second between 'this cannot be happening' and 'this is absolutely happening.'

## Assessment

Green T is what Waluigi aspires to be: someone who gets knocked down repeatedly, loses everything, and comes back MORE dangerous each time. He lost his organization to Archie's fireball and Earl Grey's explosion. He lost his freedom to the mirror dimension. He lost any pretense of belonging to a faction or having backup. And yet he kept going—surviving, adapting, and ultimately delivering one of the most satisfying moments of the entire campaign.

Waluigi respects very few people unconditionally. Green T has earned that respect. He is proof that being underestimated is not a weakness—it's a weapon. And Waluigi, who has been underestimated his entire life, finds that deeply, personally meaningful.

Waluigi would buy Green T a drink. Several drinks. And then Waluigi would ask him how he smuggled that gun into the dinner party, because Waluigi NEEDS to know. WAH.

## Recent Update — Temporary Mirror Custodian

After the mirror base and fragment were recovered, Green T became the practical custodian of the restored Mirror of True Reflection. This is not the same as ownership. Wario has opinions about ownership. Waluigi has opinions about Wario’s opinions. The important part is that the artifact is no longer broken and is currently in party control while the portal circle remains occupied by Tanukiburt, Toadburt, and Mystic Morel.

name: Commander G
title: The Iron Fist in a Velvet Glove
status: Active — commanding the Swiftsoul Chapter of the Iron Fists Guild
summary: Commander G leads the Swiftsoul Chapter of the Iron Fists Guild with ruthless efficiency and a network of contacts that spans both Kingdom officials and underworld figures. She plays all sides, maintains plausible deniability, and runs operations that blur the line between mercenary work and organized crime. She is also the mother of 'X.O.,' whose volatile personality and theatrical demands have apparently injected chaos into Guild decision-making, possibly explaining the messy Swiftsoul operation and the use of Archie Miser as a scapegoat.
description:
Commander G is the kind of leader who makes Waluigi deeply uncomfortable—not because she's evil (plenty of evil people are easy to deal with) but because she's COMPETENT in ways that make her difficult to predict, outmaneuver, or survive.

The Iron Fists Guild under her command operates with notorious autonomy in the Midlands. They take contracts from anyone who pays, provide 'security services' that sometimes look more like protection rackets, and maintain a network of informants, corrupt officials, and underworld contacts that would make any intelligence agency jealous. G herself maintains a low public profile—no dramatic speeches, no ostentatious displays of power. She focuses on results.

This pragmatism makes her dangerous. You can't appeal to her ideology because she doesn't seem to have one beyond 'profitable efficiency.' You can't exploit her emotions because she doesn't display any. You can't outbid her loyalty because her loyalty is already sold to whoever pays best this week.

## The X.O. Problem

Commander G's effectiveness is reportedly being undermined by her daughter, known in Guild communications as 'X.O.' Where G is pragmatic, X.O. is theatrical. Where G seeks efficiency, X.O. demands drama. Where G would choose the simplest solution, X.O. insists on elaborate operations that satisfy her personal aesthetic rather than operational requirements.

X.O. apparently exhibits what underworld analysts describe as 'Kamidere tendencies'—a profound god complex, narcissistic entitlement, and a belief that Guild operations exist primarily for her amusement. She reportedly demanded the 'Burn Notice' protocol for the Swiftsoul incident purely for dramatic effect, overruling more pragmatic alternatives.

The Swiftsoul operation's messiness—the obvious frame-up of Archie, the volatile cargo, the suspicious timing, the evidence trails that almost seem designed to be found—may be the result of X.O.'s influence on Guild planning. A clean operation would serve G's interests. A theatrical operation that creates chaos and leaves witnesses serves X.O.'s entertainment.

Waluigi does not know the internal dynamics of G and X.O.'s relationship. Does G indulge her daughter's demands? Is she manipulated by them? Does X.O. have leverage over her mother, or is G simply blind to her daughter's destabilizing influence? The answers matter because understanding G requires understanding what constraints she operates under—and X.O. appears to be a significant constraint.

## Guild Operations

Under G's command, the Iron Fists' Swiftsoul Chapter specializes in high-risk mercenary work:

- 'Discreet logistical support' — moving sensitive cargo without questions
- 'Asset protection/retrieval' — acquiring items or people for clients
- 'Problem resolution' — eliminating obstacles through whatever means necessary

The Guild communique recovered from the Swiftsoul investigation reveals standard operational codes: 'Burn Notice Active' (eliminate witnesses/evidence), 'Level 3 Contaminants' (high-risk targets or materials), 'Protocol Sigma-9' (cleanup procedures). These codes suggest a sophisticated organizational structure with established procedures for criminal operations.

The communique also mentions 'Wario's folly created necessary opportunity for adjustment,' suggesting G's operations intersected with Wario's schemes in ways that required rapid adaptation. Whether G was working WITH Wario, AGAINST Wario, or simply exploiting chaos Wario created is unclear.

## Assessment

Commander G is not someone Waluigi wants to confront directly. She has resources, information, and the willingness to eliminate problems permanently. The Swiftsoul operation—whatever its full scope—demonstrates her capacity for complex schemes that sacrifice pawns (like Archie) to protect larger objectives.

If Archie's defense requires exposing Guild involvement in the Swiftsoul explosion, that defense will make enemies of Commander G and her organization. This is dangerous but may be necessary. The evidence points to Guild culpability. The Guild will not appreciate that evidence being presented in court.

Waluigi recommends caution when dealing with anyone connected to Commander G. Waluigi also recommends having an exit strategy, a backup plan, and preferably a different continent to flee to if things go wrong.

WAH.

name: X.O.
title: The Divine Daughter
status: Active — wielding influence within the Iron Fists Guild through her mother Commander G
summary: X.O. is Commander G's daughter and a destabilizing influence within the Iron Fists Guild's Swiftsoul Chapter. She exhibits profound narcissistic entitlement, a god complex that would embarrass actual deities, and a tendency to view Guild operations as theatrical performances staged for her personal amusement. Her demands for dramatic, often cruel, operational protocols may be responsible for the chaotic nature of the Swiftsoul incident—including the elaborate framing of Archie Miser.
description:
Waluigi has encountered people with inflated self-images before. Waluigi HAS an inflated self-image—the difference is that Waluigi's image is ACCURATE, whereas most people's inflated self-images are delusional. X.O.'s self-image is so inflated it has achieved escape velocity. She doesn't just think she's better than everyone else. She thinks she's operating on a fundamentally different level of existence, where ordinary rules don't apply and ordinary people exist solely to validate her magnificence.

This would be merely annoying if X.O. didn't have POWER. But she does—influence over the Iron Fists Guild through her mother Commander G. When X.O. demands elaborate loyalty displays, Guild members comply. When X.O. insists on theatrical operational protocols, missions are designed to satisfy her aesthetic preferences. When X.O. decides someone is amusing or pathetic, that evaluation shapes how the Guild treats them.

## The Kamidere Profile

Underworld analysts use the term 'Kamidere' to describe X.O.'s personality type: someone who genuinely believes themselves to be divine or semi-divine, expects worship from those around them, and reacts with extreme prejudice to any perceived slight against their status. X.O. reportedly:

- Demands elaborate displays of loyalty before issuing orders, including rituals where subordinates recite poetry praising her 'celestial beauty'
- Treats Guild missions as personal entertainment, evaluating them by how much drama they produce rather than operational success
- Exhibits fascination with chaotic individuals like Wario—not romantically, but like a cat watching an amusing mouse
- Chooses targets and scapegoats based on personal whims rather than strategic value

The rumor that X.O. specifically chose Archie Miser as the Swiftsoul scapegoat because she 'disliked his shifty eyes' may sound absurd, but it fits her documented behavior pattern. X.O. doesn't need good reasons. She needs amusing ones.

## Influence on Guild Operations

The Swiftsoul incident bears hallmarks of X.O.'s influence:

- The 'Burn Notice' protocol was reportedly demanded by X.O. for dramatic effect, overruling more pragmatic options
- The elaborate framing of Archie—teleporting him to the scene, drugging him, applying tracking glyphs, leaving his signature at the blast—is theatrically excessive for a simple cleanup operation
- The timing alongside Wario's fake funeral suggests someone who appreciates dramatic irony
- The use of a melted Guild emblem at the crime scene is the kind of 'calling card' that X.O. reportedly favors

G would have arranged a clean operation: explosion, no witnesses, no evidence trails, no patsy. X.O. wanted a SHOW: an obvious villain, a dramatic chase, a desperate fugitive caught on a cliffside ledge. The messiness serves her entertainment preferences, not operational efficiency.

## Relationship with Commander G

The dynamics between G and X.O. are murky. Does G indulge her daughter's demands out of parental affection? Is she manipulated through some form of leverage? Does X.O. have information or capabilities that make her essential to Guild operations despite her destabilizing influence?

Some speculation suggests X.O.'s theatrical tendencies might actually serve Guild interests by creating chaos that obscures their real objectives. If everyone focuses on the dramatic elements—the obvious scapegoat, the flashy evidence—they might miss the quieter operations happening in the background. Whether this is G's strategy or happy accident is unknown.

## Assessment

X.O. is dangerous not because she's competent but because she's UNPREDICTABLE. Competent enemies can be anticipated. Competent enemies make decisions based on logic, self-interest, and observable patterns. X.O. makes decisions based on what will amuse her, what will feed her ego, and what will produce the most dramatic outcome.

If Archie's defense exposes Guild involvement in Swiftsoul, X.O. might react with rage—or she might find the courtroom drama entertaining. She might order retaliation—or she might be distracted by a shinier amusement. She might decide the defense attorney is annoying enough to eliminate—or amusing enough to watch.

Waluigi recommends treating any interaction with X.O. as inherently theatrical. She's always performing. She's always the hero of her own narrative. Anyone who threatens that narrative is either a villain to be destroyed or comic relief to be mocked. There is no middle ground.

WAH.

name: Kyle Coinsoul
title: The Guild Man with Gambling Debts
status: Active — Iron Fists Guild operative, potential witness in Case 4739
summary: Kyle Coinsoul is an Iron Fists Guild operative who interacted with Archie Miser shortly before the Swiftsoul explosion. He was seen using an unauthorized override key near Platform 3 and has documented gambling debts that could provide motive for complicity in Guild operations. He is a potential weak link in the Guild's involvement—someone who might flip under pressure if his debts or legal exposure make cooperation attractive.
description:
Kyle Coinsoul is the kind of mid-level operative who makes elaborate criminal conspiracies possible. He's not important enough to plan operations, but he's important enough to execute crucial steps. He's not trusted with secrets, but he's trusted with keys. He's not valuable enough to protect, but he's visible enough to become a liability.

Witnesses place Coinsoul in conversation with Archie Miser approximately 30 minutes before the Swiftsoul explosion. The official story is 'routine guild service fee' transaction. The reality, based on follow-up interviews, is that Miser was 'panicked' and 'desperate for work,' and Coinsoul was 'tense' and 'frequently glancing toward Platform 3.'

More damning: Coinsoul was seen using an unauthorized override key near Platform 3 access controls shortly after Miser departed. This key—later identified as a master override usually held by senior Guild officers or station command—gave someone access to the platform where the explosion occurred.

## The Gambling Debts

Coinsoul has documented gambling debts owed to parties that may include Iron Fists-affiliated bookmakers. This creates multiple pressure points:

- He may have participated in the Swiftsoul operation under coercion (debt forgiveness in exchange for cooperation)
- He may be vulnerable to Defense overtures (testimony in exchange for legal protection)
- He may be a target for Guild elimination (loose end who knows too much and owes too much)

Debt makes people cooperative. Debt makes people desperate. Coinsoul has both the motive to have participated in framing Archie AND the motive to betray the Guild if a better offer presents itself.

## Evidentiary Value

Coinsoul can potentially establish:

- That Archie was seeking Guild assistance BEFORE the explosion, inconsistent with premeditated attack
- That Guild personnel had access to Platform 3 via override keys
- That the Guild's presence at Platform 3 was coordinated, not coincidental
- That 'routine' explanations for Guild activity that day are fabricated

The risk is that Coinsoul may be too afraid of Guild retaliation to testify honestly, or the Guild may eliminate him before he can be deposed. Defense should move quickly to secure his testimony, potentially offering protection or debt relief as incentives.

## Assessment

Waluigi does not have strong feelings about Kyle Coinsoul specifically. He's a functionary—a gear in a larger machine. But gears can break. Gears can be removed and examined. Gears can reveal how the whole machine works.

If Archie's defense needs to prove Guild involvement, Coinsoul is where they start. He's the visible connection between Archie, the Guild, and Platform 3. Getting him to talk might unravel the entire conspiracy.

WAH.

name: Elder Rowan Meadowlight
title: The Fallen Druid
status: Deceased — died under suspicious circumstances in Veridian Grove
summary: Elder Rowan Meadowlight was a respected druid of the Veridian Grove who died on the same day as the Swiftsoul explosion, with Archie Miser found near the scene. The prosecution claims Archie caused his death through reckless magic or deliberate silencing of a witness. The defense evidence suggests the Elder was killed by a sophisticated third party who sabotaged the Grove's ancient wards specifically to frame Archie—the same people responsible for the Swiftsoul explosion.
description:
Elder Meadowlight represented something increasingly rare in the Midlands: genuine moral authority untainted by factional politics. The Veridian Grove Druid Circle stood apart from the vampire-werewolf conflicts, the Guild schemes, and the Kingdom's sometimes brutal pragmatism. They tended the land, maintained ancient protections, and offered healing to those who needed it regardless of affiliation.

Now Meadowlight is dead, and the circumstances of his death have become another piece of the elaborate frame designed to destroy Archie Miser.

## The Official Narrative

Prosecution claims: Archie fled from Swiftsoul after the explosion, traveled to Veridian Grove (perhaps following a note from someone named 'Elara'), and either deliberately killed Elder Meadowlight to silence a witness or caused his death through reckless magic.

Evidence cited: Archie was seen entering the village. Fire residue was found near the Elder's body. The timing aligns with Archie's escape.

## The Actual Evidence

The defense's examination of the scene reveals a more complex picture:

**Ward Sabotage:** The Veridian Grove's ancient protective wards—500+ years old, maintained by generations of druids—were deliberately attenuated against fire and necromantic magic approximately 5-10 minutes BEFORE Archie's arrival. This required expert knowledge of Sylvan warding architecture that Archie does not possess. Someone prepared the Grove to be vulnerable to exactly the type of magic Archie uses.

**The Elder's Staff:** The staff fragment found near Meadowlight's body shows impact damage inconsistent with fire—it was SHATTERED by kinetic force, with embedded traces of cold-forged silver alloy used in anti-druidic wardbreakers. The fire damage came AFTER the impact, as if to mask the true cause of death.

**The Secondary Event:** Witness Faelan Whisperwind reported a 'muffled pop' near the Elder's position approximately 17:45—a sound consistent with Dispel Magic targeting the residual evidence of ward manipulation. Someone was cleaning up their sabotage.

**The Metallic Traces:** The same unusual metallic contamination (silver, iron, copper) found in the Swiftsoul residue was found at the Grove. The two scenes are connected by physical evidence.

## The 'Elara' Connection

A note found in Archie's possession mentioned meeting someone named 'Elara' urgently near Veridian Grove. Intriguingly, the junior healer who treated Archie after his arrest was named Elara Meadowlight—possibly a relative of the Elder.

If 'Elara' is the same person, several questions arise:
- How did she know to contact Archie BEFORE the Swiftsoul incident?
- Was the note genuine, or was it fabricated to lure Archie to the Grove?
- Is Elara a victim, a witness, or a participant in the conspiracy?

The coincidence of names—Elara MEADOWLIGHT treating the man accused of killing Elder MEADOWLIGHT—is either remarkable or deliberate.

## Assessment

Elder Meadowlight's death was not caused by Archie Miser. The evidence points to a sophisticated operation: sabotage the wards, kill the Elder through means masked by fire, lure Archie to the scene, let him take the blame. The same people who arranged the Swiftsoul explosion arranged this death.

Why kill Meadowlight? Waluigi has theories:
- He may have had knowledge connecting the Guild to their operations
- He may have been in the way of something they wanted in the Grove
- He may simply have been a convenient additional charge to pile on Archie's frame

Whatever the reason, an innocent man is dead, and his death is being used to condemn another innocent man. The real killers remain free.

WAH.

name: Rakka
title: The Enigmatic Employer
status: Unknown — operates from a hidden temple in the enchanted woods
summary: Rakka is a mysterious figure who employs agents for dangerous retrieval missions from a hidden temple deep in the enchanted woods. Archie Miser worked for Rakka in the period leading up to the Swiftsoul incident, receiving payments for 'retrieval fees' and 'courier services.' Rakka may be connected to the teleportation that brought Archie to Swiftsoul, and the phrase 'Rakka silence protocol' in Archie's ledger suggests their relationship may have become dangerous.
description:
Nobody knows what Rakka actually IS. The rumors span the entire spectrum of supernatural possibilities: a sorceress hiding from enemies, a spirit bound to the temple, a fey entity with mortal-world ambitions, a collector of forbidden knowledge, a displaced noble playing games from exile. Waluigi has heard all of these theories and believes none of them completely.

What IS known about Rakka:

- They operate from a hidden temple deep in the enchanted woods, protected by magic that discourages outside contact
- They employ agents for tasks requiring discretion, specific skills, and willingness to accept danger
- Their tasks often involve retrieving artifacts or navigating dangerous territories
- They pay well—Archie's ledger shows 'Retrieval Fee (Partial)' and 'Courier Service' payments from 'Rakka'
- They value secrecy above almost everything else

## Archie's Employment

Archie worked for Rakka in the weeks leading up to the Swiftsoul incident. His activities during this period included:

- Missions with pirates (the Sea Dogs) and an unidentified 'horse person'
- Travel to Ravencreek, possibly for retrieval or information gathering
- Return to Rakka's Temple after the Ravencreek werewolf attack

The teleportation residue found on Archie at Swiftsoul matches traces associated with Rakka's known nexus points. This suggests Archie was teleported FROM Rakka's Temple TO Swiftsoul, arriving in a panicked state shortly before the explosion.

Was this teleportation Archie's choice? Was it Rakka's doing? Was it arranged by a third party using Rakka's infrastructure? The answers matter enormously for understanding the Swiftsoul conspiracy.

## The 'Silence Protocol'

Archie's encoded ledger contains a disturbing entry: 'Contingency Gamma: Druid Contact Necessary if FG double-cross suspected re: Quill cargo OR Rakka silence protocol initiated.'

This suggests Archie anticipated potential betrayal from Rakka as well as from the Fighter's Guild. A 'silence protocol' implies elimination of loose ends—and Archie, having worked multiple missions for Rakka, would certainly know things worth silencing.

Did Rakka turn on Archie? Did the Iron Fists manipulate Rakka's resources to teleport Archie to Swiftsoul? Is Rakka a victim of the same conspiracy that targeted Archie, or a participant in it?

## Assessment

Rakka remains an unknown quantity. They possess significant magical resources (the teleportation network), operate with complete secrecy, and may have motives that connect to the Swiftsoul conspiracy in ways not yet understood.

Waluigi recommends treating Rakka as neither ally nor enemy until more information is available.
